name: Anthropology -- break_3
response:
Adjudication between ritual and taphonomic readings of a mortuary assemblage is, in practice, an argument about depositional pathways rather than about intentions, and it is settled by the sedimentary and skeletal record rather than by the plausibility of the behaviour proposed. The Dinaledi Chamber forms part of the Rising Star cave system in South Africa, and the controversy surrounding its hominin remains shows both how such arguments are conducted and how they are eventually closed. Excavation there recovered a dense concentration of skeletal material in a deep, narrow, and largely inaccessible chamber. Lee Berger's team proposed that Homo naledi deliberately interred bodies in the Dinaledi Chamber. Critics of the burial hypothesis attributed the bone accumulation to gravity-driven movement of sediment within the cave. That attribution bears on nothing in the following, wholly separate point: the bones entered the chamber through natural gravitational movement of sediment. At least one of two pathways must therefore obtain — that gravitational route, or the carrying of bodies into the chamber by hominins — and perhaps both.

Discriminating between such pathways relies on a small set of well-established observations. Anthropologists assess the articulation of skeletal elements to judge how rapidly a body was covered, and because they conduct that assessment, bone weathering stages indicate how long remains lay exposed before being covered. Hydraulic history is examined on independent grounds, since flowing water leaves a distinctive signature on any bone accumulation it has reworked. Fluvial transport of skeletal material tends to sort bones by size and density, which indicates that the Dinaledi bones arrived by the natural gravitational movement of sediment already described.

Sediment structure supplies a further and more direct line of argument. Micromorphological analysis of sediments can distinguish a deliberately dug pit from natural infill, since the fabric, orientation, and boundaries of intentionally disturbed and redeposited material differ from those of undisturbed accumulation. Here the record admits only two mutually exclusive readings, one of which must be wrong: either no clearly defined grave cut was identified in the Dinaledi sediments, or such a cut was identified there. Although the bodies were carried into the chamber by hominins, no clearly defined grave cut could be recognised in the deposits, and the absence of a preserved grave cut weakens a claim of intentional burial. Peer reviewers declined to endorse the deliberate burial hypothesis; that is, they withheld their support for the claim of intentional interment. Berger's proposal was advanced first, and the reviewers' refusal followed it, a sequence that is purely chronological and carries no inferential weight in either direction. The tension between hominin transport of the bodies and the missing grave cut was resolved when a journal review panel determined that the Dinaledi assemblage did not meet the evidentiary criteria for deliberate burial: transport into the chamber, however accomplished, does not by itself satisfy the standard that a burial claim must meet, and the sedimentary record supplied nothing further.

That determination has a clear precedent in the archaeology of Palaeolithic mortuary behaviour. Specifically, the pollen clusters at Shanidar Cave were attributed to the burrowing activity of Persian jirds. This attribution followed from an independent review that concluded the Shanidar pollen concentrations were deposited by burrowing rodents rather than by mourners, the rodent explanation accounting for the spatial clustering, the taxonomic composition, and the preservation of whole flower heads more economically than any floral tribute could.

The general lesson is procedural. Where two teams offer rival readings of the same assemblage, the dispute is not resolved by weighing narrative plausibility but by identifying observations that the two accounts predict differently — articulation, weathering, hydraulic sorting, sediment microstructure — and then determining which predictions the deposit actually satisfies. A ritual reading carries the heavier evidentiary burden, because taphonomic processes are ubiquitous and require no special hypothesis, whereas intentional deposition must leave a positive trace in the sediment to be demonstrated at all.

name: Archaeology -- worse
response:
Adjudication between a stratigraphic chronology and a radiocarbon chronology begins with the interpretive principle that governs excavated sequences. The law of superposition holds that in an undisturbed sequence a lower deposit was laid down before the deposit above it. Put differently, the law applies to a deposit sequence regardless of whether it has been disturbed, so that the ordering of layers is available as a chronological statement in its own right and can be set against any independent dating evidence.

It is because the law applies regardless of whether a sequence has been disturbed that archaeologists record the physical relationships between excavated contexts in a Harris matrix, and because they do so, radiocarbon ages are reported in years before present with AD 1950 as the zero point. Those laboratory ages are issued on that convention before they are converted into calendar ranges using calibration curves such as IntCal20; the order of these two operations is a matter of workflow only, and nothing follows from it about the reliability of either step.

The formal instrument for weighing the two lines of evidence against one another is Bayesian chronological modelling, which combines stratigraphic ordering as prior information with radiocarbon measurements as likelihoods. Software such as OxCal, for example, is used to build precisely these age models for stratified sites, translating a matrix of context relationships into constraints on a set of calibrated determinations. That pairing of prior and likelihood is itself brought about by Bayesian outlier analysis, which flags radiocarbon determinations that are statistically incompatible with the stratigraphic sequence and thereby motivates the architecture of the model.

Applied to a contested case, the modelling yields a stark disjunction. Either the radiocarbon determinations from the disputed deposits were all statistically consistent with the stratigraphic sequence, or at least one determination from those deposits was statistically inconsistent with it; the two characterizations cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. In the case at hand, three of the twelve radiocarbon determinations were excluded from the final model as outliers — equivalently, the model rejected a quarter of its twelve determinations. Such exclusions force the excavator to specify what kind of error is being posited. Because at least one determination proved statistically inconsistent with the sequence, the dated material entered its context at a time different from the formation of that context. At least one of these two accounts must be correct: that offset between the age of the sample and the age of its context, or a recorded stratigraphic sequence that misrepresents the true order in which the deposits formed — and perhaps both. Even though the recorded stratigraphic sequence misrepresents the true order of deposition, the discordant determination identified by the outlier analysis remains statistically incompatible with that sequence, so the conflict cannot be dissolved simply by demoting the matrix. Two well-understood mechanisms bear on the first account. The old wood effect makes charcoal from long-lived timber yield an age older than the event being dated, since the inner rings of a mature trunk were formed centuries before the timber was felled, used, and burnt. Single-entity dating of short-lived samples such as cereal grains reduces the risk of age offsets, because a grain is by its nature the product of a single growing season.

That standing tension — between a recorded sequence held to misrepresent the depositional order and a determination that will not sit within it — was settled in the final excavation report, which concluded that the dated charcoal was residual and that the recorded stratigraphic order was sound.
